name: Opus-fleet deep value
strategy: Concentrated in sub-market-multiple, FCF-rich dividend payers at 10-13x forward earnings (energy, pharma/healthcare, a cheap bank, telecom), tilted toward the commodity/inflation re-acceleration now visible in the tape, hedged by a small short in expensive no-growth consumer-staples bond proxies.
reassessment_note: Three things changed my mind this week. (1) A commodity/inflation re-acceleration is now unambiguous on the tape: crude CL=F +10.2% in a month to $85.18, USO +19.4% 1m and +9.5% this week, DBC +10.5% 1m, GLD +4.4% 1m with GDX +18.3% and NEM +21.7% -- and simultaneously the long end sold off, 10y 4.78% (+11bp on the month) and 30y 5.28%. Gold and commodities rallying alongside RISING nominal long rates is a real-rate/debasement signal, and that regime is the single best backdrop there is for short-duration cheap cash flows over long-duration multiples. My cohort is the direct beneficiary and I was underexposed to it sitting on 32% cash. XLE/SPY relative strength is now in a confirmed uptrend (rel > 50dma > 200dma), +9.9% relative in a month. So I raise energy from 18% to 25% and cut cash from 32% to 22%, lifting gross from 68% to 78%. (2) I am covering the SMH short and admitting it was the wrong expression of the hedge. The 'stretched growth cohort' I meant to short is not semis: semis are a cyclical in a violent earnings upcycle where multiples are COMPRESSING as EPS explodes -- SNDK +2684% 12m, MU +720%, WDC +417%, STX +365%, INTC +289%, and SMH beat SPY by 2.4% this week alone while my leg bled -1.86% in four sessions. SMH/SPY relative trend is mixed, not broken. Shorting a squeeze in a memory supercycle is not deep value, it is just paying the funding to be run over. (3) The correct short for THIS mandate in THIS regime is the expensive defensive bond proxy. XLP trades at 22.2x for zero earnings growth, its two largest holdings are WMT (9.6%) and COST (8.9%) at premium retail multiples, it faces a direct COGS hit from commodities up 10% in a month, and it is discounted against a 5.28% 30-year. Unlike SMH it is already confirmed rolling over: XLP/SPY is in a clean relative downtrend (rel < 50dma < 200dma), -1.1% relative this week, -13.3% over six months. That is a value manager's short -- expensive cash flows against my cheap ones -- not a momentum fight. I also broaden single-name risk: PFE cut 22 to 14 and the freed weight spread across BMY, CVS and XOM rather than concentrated in one patent cliff. I keep 22% cash because SKEW is at 151.6, up 16.9 points in a month, while VIX sits at 14.5 -- someone is paying up for tails under a calm index, and SPY has gone nowhere for a month (+0.21%) after +15.2% in six.

positions.thesis: Core integrated energy and my largest position. Crude is re-accelerating (+10.2% in a month to $85.18) and CVX is capturing it: +11.2% over the month, +12.3% over three, and only 1.5% off its 52-week high -- among the strongest risk-adjusted charts in the book at 25% realized vol. This is a ~4% dividend yield backed by one of the best free-cash-flow conversion profiles in the majors and a balance sheet that funds the payout below $60 crude, so I am paid to wait even if the commodity move stalls. Sized at 15% because it is the highest-conviction intersection of my mandate (FCF-rich dividend payer) and the macro signal (inflation re-acceleration), but held below 20% because it is still a single commodity bet. No take-profit: this is a compounder I want to let run in a regime that favors it.

The cheapest large-cap dividend payer I can find: 10.3x forward earnings and a 6.05% yield, which is 127bp above the 30-year Treasury -- an equity paying more than the long bond while retaining upside. The whole pharma cohort is quietly re-rating around it (XPH +27.8% over three months, PPH +33.8% over twelve, XLV +12.6% over three), and PFE participated with +8.6% over the month while sitting just 2.0% off its 52-week high. The 37x trailing versus 10.3x forward is the patent-cliff trough rolling out of the numbers. Trimmed from 22% to 14% not because the thesis weakened but because it was an unnecessarily large single-name bet on one pipeline; I now express the same cheap-pharma view across PFE, BMY and CVS. Wide 18% stop because a 6% yielder deserves room to be volatile.

Still the cheapest of the large US banks at 11.8x forward, and the yield-curve news this week is directly in its favor: the 30-year at 5.28% against 3-month bills at 3.76% is a ~152bp positive slope, which is net-interest-margin expansion for a bank funded short and lent long. C added +3.6% this week and +4.63% since my 8/31 entry, outperforming XLF (flat on the week), and the restructuring story keeps producing (China brokerage licence expected this month, Kard acquisition closed). I am trimming from 14% to 11% for one honest reason: after +30.6% in six months and +44.9% in twelve, Citi is no longer the below-tangible-book asset that made it a deep-value holding -- the discount has substantially closed, so the position should shrink even though the thesis is still working. 20% stop reflects its 28% realized vol.

The higher-torque half of my energy barrel: a pure E&P with the best balance sheet in the group, at 13.5x forward with a 2.5% base dividend plus variable returns of capital. It is the strongest energy name on the tape -- +15.8% over the month and +15.4% over three, versus XLE +10.1% and XOM +3.7% -- and it sits only 2.1% off its 52-week high, so I am buying strength, not catching a knife. Paired with CVX it gives me upstream leverage to crude that an integrated's downstream margin cannot provide, which matters if the move is genuinely supply-driven. Sized at 10% behind CVX because its 31% realized vol is meaningfully higher. I attach a 45% take-profit here specifically because E&P is the leg most likely to give me a violent commodity-driven overshoot worth banking.

Deep-value healthcare with a live catalyst already delivered: 11.9x forward earnings, 2.75% yield, and management RAISED full-year guidance at the August 5 Q2 print. The sell-side has been marking up into it (JPMorgan to $118, Argus to $114) against a $96.74 price -- roughly 18-20% to consensus, the widest gap to target of anything I own. The stock added +4.0% this week and is still 12.0% below its 52-week high, so unlike C the discount has NOT closed. This is the classic deep-value setup my mandate is built for: a broken-narrative franchise where the cash flows are already re-accelerating but the multiple has not caught up. Held at 8% and stopped at 20% because managed-care earnings are genuinely hard to forecast and the cohort around it is choppy (UNH 9% off its high, CI 7.6%).

The cheapest large pharma on forward earnings at 10.4x with a 3.77% yield, up +18.0% over three months and sitting 1.9% off its 52-week high -- a second, independent draw on the same cheap-pharma re-rating that is working for PFE, but with a different pipeline and a different patent calendar, which is exactly the diversification I wanted when I cut PFE. It is deliberately my smallest long at 7% and carries my tightest equity stop at 16% because the research this week surfaced two real overhangs I am not going to pretend away: the company halted autoimmune trials over deaths or life-threatening side effects, and a federal appeals court revived the $6.7bn Celgene CVR lawsuit. Consensus target of $66.21 sits essentially at the $66.82 price, so I am buying the valuation and the yield, not a promised re-rating. Small size is the honest expression of that.

The laggard trade inside a breaking-out sector -- the most reliably deep-value way to add energy after a move has already started. XOM returned just +3.7% over the past month while XLE did +10.1%, COP +15.8% and SLB +11.2%, and it sits 5.8% below its 52-week high versus CVX at 1.5% and COP at 2.1%. Yet it is no more expensive at 12.9x forward with a 2.58% yield, and the project pipeline keeps compounding (Rovuma LNG contracts awarded, Permian midstream expansion with Targa, Venezuela optionality). At 26.2% realized vol it is the lowest-volatility way to lift energy from 18% to 25% of the book, so it does the sizing work without adding proportionate risk. Kept to 5% because it is the third energy name and I do not want the sector past a quarter of the book.

Retained but deliberately trimmed to a token 4%. The valuation case is intact -- roughly 9x earnings on a 6%+ dividend yield covered by real free cash flow, and it has quietly done +6.7% over the month and +12.4% over three while holding within 0.9% of its 52-week high. But the central macro fact of this week cuts against it: the 30-year at 5.28% and the 10-year at 4.78% and rising make a high-yield, no-growth telecom a bond substitute competing directly against an actual bond that just got cheaper. The same rate move is why I refuse to own utilities here (XLU -6.6% over six months) and why I am short staples. VZ survives the cut where those do because its multiple is half theirs, but it earns the smallest long slot and the tightest stop in the book at 12%.

This replaces the SMH short and is the mirror image of everything I am long. XLP trades at 22.2x earnings for a cohort with essentially no earnings growth, while my longs sit at 10-13x forward -- so the pair is long cheap cash flows, short expensive ones, which is the purest statement of a deep-value mandate. Three forces now press on it at once: commodity inflation running +10.5% in a month straight into staples COGS, a 30-year at 5.28% repricing every bond-proxy multiple, and its two largest holdings being WMT at 9.6% and COST at 8.9% -- premium-multiple retailers, not defensives. Crucially, and unlike SMH, the breakdown is already confirmed rather than hypothetical: XLP/SPY relative strength is below its 50-day which is below its 200-day, -1.1% relative this week and -13.3% over six months, with the constituents cracking individually (CPB -8.6%, GIS -7.8%, SJM -4.7%, PM -4.9% on the week). At 0.48 beta this is a low-volatility relative-value short, not a market hedge, so I keep it to 4% and cap the loss at 10%; 12% take-profit banks a full de-rating.
